questions.question: Does the Next.js App Router ship a built-in i18n routing system?
options: Yes, it's enabled by default for every project
No — it provides routing primitives (dynamic segments, proxy) that you use to build locale routing yourself
Only when using the Pages Router
questions.explanation: There's no built-in i18n router; a `[locale]` dynamic segment plus proxy logic is the standard way to implement locale-prefixed routing.

questions.question: What does wrapping every route under an `app/[locale]/` segment achieve?
options: It makes the app automatically translate all text
URLs like /en/courses/react and /fr/courses/react resolve to the same page.tsx, with the locale available as a route param
It disables static generation for all routes
It's required for the proxy to work at all
questions.explanation: The dynamic segment captures the locale from the URL so a single page.tsx can render per-locale content based on that param.

questions.question: Where should locale-detection-and-redirect logic (based on a visitor's browser preference) run, and why?
options: Inside the page component, after render
In the proxy, since it needs to run before any route renders
It's not possible to detect browser language in Next.js
questions.explanation: The proxy runs ahead of routing, making it the right place to redirect a visitor to a locale-prefixed URL before any page work begins.

questions.question: Why load translation dictionaries via a per-locale dynamic `import()` rather than importing all of them upfront?
options: Dynamic imports are required syntax in Next.js
A visitor only downloads the dictionary for their own locale, instead of shipping every language's strings to every visitor
It has no effect on bundle size
Static imports don't work with JSON files
questions.explanation: Per-locale dynamic imports mean a French visitor's bundle never includes the English or Hindi dictionary, keeping payload size down.
